title: The lost princess
hook: Rebbe Nachman's tale of a viceroy who searches for years for a lost princess

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rebbe Nachman's very narrow bridge, and the main thing, not to make yourself afraid. Today, the same rebbe tells a story, the first of his famous tales.

One careless sentence, said in anger, and a king loses his daughter. That's how the first of Rebbe Nachman's tales begins. He didn't only teach. In his last years he started telling stories, fairy tales really: kings and princesses, giants, deserts, enchanted palaces. They can sound like bedtime stories. He treated them as anything but: his student Nathan wrote them down, and Breslov tradition reads them as teachings in disguise.
screen: `ONE CARELESS SENTENCE.` → `A REBBE TELLS FAIRY TALES.` → `KINGS, GIANTS, PALACES.`

segments.voice: Here's the story, in short strokes. A king has a daughter he loves dearly. One day, angry with her, he blurts out: may the not-good take you. The next morning, she's gone. The king is heartbroken. His viceroy, his second-in-command, asks for a servant, a horse and some money, and sets out to find her. He searches for years. At last he finds her, held in a strange palace. She tells him how to free her: choose a place, long for her for a whole year, and on the last day, fast and stay awake. On the last day, he sees an apple, eats it, and falls into a deep sleep. He fails. She gives him a second chance: this time he may eat, but he must not drink wine. He finds a spring that looks and smells like wine, drinks, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, she's been taken farther away. All that's left is her kerchief, with a message written in her tears: now look for me on a mountain of gold, in a castle of pearl. So he gets up and keeps searching, through deserts and giants. The tale's last line is strange: how he freed her, the story doesn't tell. But in the end, he freed her. Breslov teachers read the princess as the Divine Presence in exile, and the viceroy as every person who has lost something holy and is trying to find it again. He isn't a hero because he never fails. He fails twice, badly. He's a hero because the story always says the same thing next: and he kept searching.
screen: `ONE ANGRY SENTENCE.` · `YEARS OF SEARCHING.` · `AN APPLE. A SPRING. SEVENTY YEARS.` · `A MESSAGE WRITTEN IN TEARS.` · then, large: `KEEP SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: Think of something good you once had and lost track of: a friendship, a habit, a sense of wonder, a way of praying. Don't scold yourself for falling asleep on it; the viceroy slept seventy years and still got up. Just ask where you might look for it now, one place, one small first step, and if you pray, ask for help finding it.
Viceroy, the king's second-in-command who set out to find a lost princess in Rebbe Nachman's first tale, failing, sleeping, waking, and searching until he found what was lost.
Your line: keep searching. Failing twice, even sleeping seventy years, doesn't end the story. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Rebbe Nachman's thirteen tales, collected as Sippurei Ma'asiyot, are read and studied by Breslov Hasidim and many others, often with commentaries that explain their hidden meanings.

original.note: Hebrew: the loss of a king's daughter, the name of Rebbe Nachman's first tale.

trapdoor: what you thought: a fairy tale about a princess.
what it means: a story about losing something precious and refusing to stop looking, even after failing.
what a scholar hears: the first of the Sippurei Ma'asiyot (printed in Hebrew and Yiddish), read by Breslov as the exile of the Shekhinah and the soul's search to restore it.
